title: Patenting Quantum Computing Innovations: Lessons from Four Core Quantum Algorithms - Part 1 - Quantum Computing Report
gist: A Covington & Burling special counsel argues that the U.S. Mayo/Alice patent-eligibility framework is imprecise enough to threaten IP protection for quantum computing inventions, and gives concrete claim-drafting rules — recite specific hardware and steps, not general results — to survive it. He also frames today's multi-modality quantum hardware race as analogous to the late-1980s ISDN/DSL/GSM transmission-technology contest, implying a comparable multi-decade expansion. Note the byline: the raw author field is Doug Finke but the piece is written by Sinan Utku.

themes.theme: Patent eligibility as a commercialization risk

insights.claim: Many patent practitioners believe the current U.S. rules for determining patent eligibility are murky, produce inconsistent results, and could operate as barriers to innovation and commercialization in fast-moving technology areas like quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: IP uncertainty is an under-modeled risk in quantum company valuations — moats assumed from patents may not survive a Section 101 challenge.
insights.quote: Many practitioners believe the current U.S. rules for determining patent eligibility are particularly murky and lead to inconsistent results.
insights.locator: Not all innovations, however, are eligible for patenting

insights.claim: Patent eligibility rules are not harmonized across jurisdictions, so the same quantum computing invention can be protectable in one patent system and ineligible in another.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Cross-border IP arbitrage matters: a quantum firm's portfolio strength can differ sharply by geography, affecting licensing and litigation exposure.
insights.locator: Patent granting jurisdictions have specific rules

insights.claim: Under 35 U.S. § 101 the statutory language suggests broad eligibility for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, but the U.S. Supreme Court has judicially restricted that scope with exceptions for abstract ideas, laws of nature and natural phenomena.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The gap between statute and case law is where litigation risk lives; legislative reform of §101 would be a repricing event for software-adjacent IP.
insights.locator: In the U.S., 35 U.S. § 101

insights.claim: In several decisions from 2010 to 2014 the U.S. Supreme Court imposed subject-matter eligibility restrictions more onerous than most practitioners had previously understood from earlier case law.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Patents filed under pre-2010 assumptions may be weaker than their owners' balance sheets imply.
insights.locator: Most recently, in several decisions from 2010 to 2014

insights.claim: The Mayo/Alice framework first asks whether claims are directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon or abstract idea, and if so whether they contain an 'inventive concept' amounting to significantly more than a patent on the ineligible concept itself.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: This is the exact gate every quantum algorithm patent must pass; portfolio due diligence should be scored against both steps.
insights.quote: whether the claims contain “an element or combination of elements that is ‘sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.’”
insights.locator: In particular, under the more recent Mayo/Alice framework

insights.claim: Based on a large body of court decisions over the years, many practitioners believe the Mayo/Alice framework lacks precision and is fraught with uncertainty, producing outcomes they consider counterintuitive.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Expect continued Federal Circuit volatility; IP-heavy quantum valuations carry a wider confidence interval than typical deep-tech.
insights.locator: Based on a large number of patent eligibility decisions

insights.claim: In American Axle the Federal Circuit found a claim to a driveline shaft manufacturing method ineligible because it was directed to a general application of Hooke's law and was not limited to any particular way of achieving the result, covering all methods and structures for doing so.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Physics-formula-based inventions — the essence of quantum hardware claims — are demonstrably vulnerable; this is the closest precedent to a quantum gate claim.
insights.locator: Claim Ineligible for Being Directed to a Natural Law

insights.claim: In American Axle step two, the court found no inventive concept because the claim omitted steps relating to the specific design of the apparatus — a liner damping two vibration modes simultaneously — even though that apparatus detail existed in the invention.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Eligibility can turn entirely on drafting choices rather than the underlying invention — a cheap fix that most technical founders skip.
insights.locator: The court in step two found that the claim failed

insights.claim: In the Symantec case a virus-screening claim was held ineligible because the court treated virus screening as a long-prevalent, routine and conventional abstract idea and viewed the telephone network merely as a generic environment for carrying it out.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Running a known process on novel hardware is not enough — quantum implementations of classical tasks face the same 'generic environment' attack.
insights.locator: Claim Ineligible for Being Directed to an Abstract Idea

insights.claim: Practitioners disagreed with the Symantec outcome because the invention improved known virus screening by moving detection to a network node away from both calling and called parties, avoiding virus-laden data delivery and frequent per-party database updates.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Demonstrable technical improvement does not guarantee eligibility — an argument for trade secrets alongside patents in quantum software.
insights.locator: Many practitioners disagreed with this outcome

insights.claim: Quantum developers are advised not to draft patent claims that recite a general result, but instead to recite specific steps for achieving the result, because courts find claims covering all methods of achieving a result particularly problematic.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence question for any quantum investment: are the key claims result-based or step-based?
insights.locator: Recommendations for Quantum Developers

insights.claim: Particularizing a claim to specific hardware, or to steps carried out by specific hardware, materially helps in arguing patent eligibility.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Hardware-tied claims are narrower but survivable — implies quantum IP moats will be modality-specific rather than algorithm-wide.
insights.locator: In particular, courts find claims that cover all methods

insights.claim: Including enough detail in the written description to support an argument that the invention improves an existing technological process or improves the device carrying it out is helpful in demonstrating patent eligibility.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Specification quality, not just claim text, determines defensibility — a checkable artifact in IP diligence.
insights.locator: Providing enough detail in the patent application

insights.claim: Where claims must include mathematical or physics formulae or general scientific principles, they should recite specific applications of those principles in the context of a specific device or method.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Directly applicable to quantum gate and error-correction patents, which are inherently formula-driven.
insights.locator: If the claims will include mathematical or physics formulae

insights.claim: The great variation in quantum hardware approaches being pursued simultaneously — superconductors, photonics, trapped ions, quantum dots and others — is presented as a sign that important discoveries will likely occur in the near future.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Reframes modality fragmentation as bullish signal rather than immaturity — a contrarian read versus 'no winner yet, so stay out'.
insights.locator: Historical Comparison of the Current State of Quantum Computing

insights.claim: It is not clear whether only one quantum technology will eventually prevail or whether multiple viable quantum computers will develop in competition with one another.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Supports a basket approach across modalities rather than concentrated single-technology bets.
insights.locator: It is not clear whether eventually only one of these will prevail

insights.claim: Today's quantum field is compared to consumer digital transmission technologies of the late 1980s, when ISDN, Ethernet, DSL variants, GSM, IS-54, IS-36 and wireless LAN technologies were all actively pursued at once.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The analogy implies many competing quantum platforms coexist in niches rather than one winner — and that the value accrues over decades, not quarters.
insights.locator: In this respect, the current state of the field bears some resemblance

insights.claim: In the 1980s transmission analogy some technologies reached dead ends and were abandoned while many evolved into current niches, and the competitive activity itself drove technological advancement and economic activity with global impact over fifty years.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Sets the base rate: expect write-offs among quantum modalities alongside a much larger aggregate economic expansion.
insights.locator: As we know now, some of these technologies reached dead ends

insights.claim: The simultaneous pursuit of different quantum technologies may be a harbinger of technological and economic expansion comparable to the fifty-year impact of digital transmission technologies.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A long-duration thesis: sizing quantum against the telecom buildout rather than against a single product cycle.
insights.locator: The current simultaneous pursuit of different technologies

themes.theme: Where the eligibility line actually falls

insights.claim: Most practitioners would agree a computer program controlling an apparatus in an industrially useful process should be eligible, while a program specified purely as data manipulation under an algorithm with no nexus to a specific industrial apparatus or process should not be.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Places pure quantum algorithm patents near the ineligible pole and QPU-control patents near the eligible pole — a portfolio sorting rule.
insights.locator: More arguable issues of patent eligibility arise

insights.claim: The policy rationale for refusing eligibility to abstract computational claims is pre-emption: a broad patent on something like unit conversion would wholesale block activities in biotechnology, mechanical technologies and hi-tech that require the same operation.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Understanding the pre-emption logic predicts which broad quantum-algorithm claims will be struck down.
insights.locator: Otherwise, activities in entirely different fields

insights.claim: There is a vast spectrum of computer-implemented inventions between the clearly eligible and clearly ineligible extremes in which eligibility is genuinely unclear, and quantum computing inventions sit inside that gray zone.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Means outcomes hinge on counsel quality and drafting discipline — a differentiator between otherwise similar quantum startups.
insights.locator: There is a vast spectrum of computer-implemented inventions

insights.claim: The article is authored by Sinan Utku, Special Counsel at Covington and Burling LLP and an instructor at Bilkent University Law School, writing in a personal capacity, and is the first of a five-part weekly series covering a Pauli Z gate, a surface-code logical qubit, entanglement swapping and Shor's algorithm as worked eligibility examples.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Signals that top-tier IP counsel now treat quantum §101 exposure as a distinct practice area; the later parts will name specific claim archetypes to stress-test.
insights.locator: Sinan Utku is a Special Counsel
